hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever been so hungry it changed how you treated people?
options: same. hold onto that. this one is about what hunger can teach.
that’s honest. listen to this one.
then you’re ahead of most of us. listen anyway.

steps.line: In the early days of the fast in Medina, the rule was stricter: if you fell asleep after sunset before eating, no more food until the next sunset.
A man named Qays worked all day in his palm grove, fasting. At sunset he came home, and his wife went out to find him some food.

steps.q: He’s exhausted, and the food isn’t ready yet. What do you think happens?
o: His wife wakes him and he eats
He falls asleep and misses his meal
He eats a few dates in secret
steps.why: When his wife came back and found him asleep, she said, “Oh no, you’ve lost out!” (Bukhari 1915). Under the rule, sleep meant no food till the next sunset.

steps.line: Worn out, he fell asleep before she came back. So he fasted on through the next day, and by midday he fainted.
Then a verse came: eat and drink through the night, until the white thread of dawn shows clear from the black thread of night.

steps.q: Why might this verse have come right after Qays’s story?
o: To show the fast is meant to be livable
To reward Qays for his patience
To punish those who broke the old rule
steps.why: The night was opened for eating, drinking and rest. “God wants ease for you, not hardship,” the Qur’an says of the fast (2:185).

steps.q: One man, ‘Adi, hears the verse about the white and black threads. What do you think he does?
o: Puts real threads under his pillow
Waits each dawn for a sign in the sky
Stays awake until the call to prayer
steps.why: ‘Adi ibn Hatim laid a white and a black thread under his pillow and kept checking all night. He couldn’t tell them apart (Bukhari 1916).

steps.line: One man named ‘Adi took it literally. He put a white thread and a black thread under his pillow, and kept checking all night. He couldn’t tell them apart.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ teased him gently: then your pillow must be very wide! The threads, he explained, are the dark of night and the light of day.
Today, Muslims still eat suhoor in the dark before dawn, fast all day, and break the fast at sunset, often with a date and water.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Many Muslims break the fast with a date and water. Why dates?
o: Dates were the only food in Medina
The Prophet ﷺ broke his fast that way
steps.why: Abu Dawud records he broke his fast with fresh dates, or dried ones, or if none, sips of water. Millions copy that small habit every sunset.

say: here’s what i love. when the fast was too hard on a tired farmer, the rule became gentler. and a too-literal pillow got a smile, not a scolding.
the qur’an says the fast is for taqwa, a careful awareness of God. in islam the hunger is a tool, not the point.

steps.q: The Prophet ﷺ said: if someone won’t give up lying, God has no need of their giving up food and drink. What does that say about the fast?
o: Lying cancels the fast like eating does
The fast is for the whole self, not just the stomach
God cares about words, not food
steps.why: Most scholars say lying doesn’t technically break the fast, but it empties it. The hunger is a tool for taqwa, a careful awareness of God.

today.say: try a small fast of the tongue today: no sharp or untrue word until sunset. when one comes up, let it go, the way the fast lets the food go.
options: lovely. that’s the part of the fast that goes with you all year.
that counts. one hour of careful words is real.

sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1915 (al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib: the early rule about sleeping before eating; Qays ibn Sirma al-Ansari, the palm grove, falling asleep before his wife returned, fainting at midday; the revelation of Qur’an 2:187)
Qur’an 2:187 (eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread of the dawn), paraphrased
Sahih al-Bukhari 1916; 4509–4510 (‘Adi ibn Hatim’s white and black threads under his pillow; “your pillow is very wide”; the darkness of night and the whiteness of day)
Qur’an 2:183 (fasting prescribed “that ye may ward off (evil)”: taqwa)
Qur’an 2:184–185 (the sick and travelers excused; “Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you”, 2:185)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1903 (whoever does not give up false speech, God has no need of his leaving food and drink)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1923; Sahih Muslim 1095 (suhoor); Sunan Abi Dawud 2356 (breaking the fast with dates and water)
check: The man’s name: Bukhari 1915 gives Qays ibn Sirma; other reports give Sirma ibn Qays or Abu Qays. Confirm “a man named Qays”.
Bukhari 1915 says only that he worked during the day; “his palm grove” (and painting RA1) follows other reports that he worked among the palms. Confirm.
The ‘Adi ibn Hatim hadith: “your pillow must be very wide” follows Bukhari 4509 (“your pillow is wide”); 4510 has “your neck is wide”. Confirm “teased him gently” as the tone.
Bukhari 1915 also mentions the related change about marital relations at night (2:187); the lesson leaves it out for a general audience, as the day-6 script does.
